strengths: Extensive empirical evaluation across multiple datasets (NeRF-DS, D-NeRF, HyperNeRF, Nerfies, iPhone) and the full 50-scene MonoDyGauBench, with per-scene breakdowns and ablations on pruning percentages and group counts in the appendix, giving strong evidence for the claimed speedups.

The three proposed components (TSP, TSS, GroupFlow) are complementary and individually motivated: TSP generalizes established static-scene Hessian/gradient pruning to the temporal domain in a principled way, TSS provides a lightweight self-supervised mechanism to expose temporally unstable Gaussians, and GroupFlow offers an interpretable, efficient rigid-motion distillation strategy grounded in classical registration (Umeyama alignment).

The reported efficiency gains are substantial and consistent (6-30x rendering speedup, 10x+ fewer Gaussians, 2-4x faster training) while largely preserving or even slightly improving image quality metrics (PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS) relative to the DeformableGS baseline, which is a meaningful practical contribution for real-time dynamic 3DGS.

The paper is generally well written and organized, with clear mathematical formulations for each module and helpful figures/visual comparisons illustrating floater suppression and rendering quality trade-offs.

The method is architecture-agnostic to a reasonable degree (TSP/TSS apply to any dynamic 3DGS framework; GroupFlow to those with explicit motion fields), which broadens potential applicability beyond DeformableGS/4DGS.
weaknesses: The technical novelty is somewhat incremental: TSP is a direct temporal extension of Speedy-Splat/PUP3D-GS pruning scores, TSS is a straightforward jittered-timestamp regularization, and GroupFlow's clustering + Umeyama alignment is a fairly standard rigid registration procedure; the core contribution is the combination and application to dynamic 3DGS rather than fundamentally new techniques.

Some quality degradation is evident in several settings (e.g., 4DGS+Pruning+GroupFlow drops PSNR from 23.55 to 21.00 on MonoDyGauBench, iPhone dataset PSNR drops with pruning, D-NeRF pruning reduces PSNR by ~2-3dB), and while acknowledged as a limitation, the paper does not deeply analyze failure cases or provide guidance on when GroupFlow's rigid-motion assumption breaks down for highly non-rigid content beyond a brief mention.

The self-reported comparison baselines (EffGS, STG, RTGS) are taken directly from MonoDyGauBench and not independently re-verified with the authors' pipeline, and the standalone SpeeDe3DGS codebase results differ from the MonoDyGauBench-wrapped results (as noted in Appendix A.6), raising questions about which numbers are most representative and complicating reproducibility/comparability across the two reported settings.

GroupFlow's control point selection (farthest point sampling) and group assignment via a similarity score are heuristic and their sensitivity/robustness to scene structure or camera-pose noise is not deeply analyzed beyond the group-count ablation; no comparison against alternative clustering schemes is provided.

Training-time comparisons are conducted on different GPUs (RTX 3090 for baselines vs RTX A5000/A6000 for the proposed method) due to memory constraints, which, although explained, makes precise training-time speedup claims (e.g., 2.53x) less rigorous as a controlled comparison.

The paper does not report any measure of variance/uncertainty in the tables (e.g., standard deviation over the three repeated runs) despite mentioning results are averaged over three runs, limiting statistical assessment of significance of small gains (e.g., SSIM improvements of 0.001-0.002).

strengths: Extensive empirical evaluation spanning the 50-scene MonoDyGauBench, NeRF-DS, D-NeRF, and HyperNeRF datasets, with per-scene breakdowns and multiple ablations (pruning percentages, number of GroupFlow groups) reported in the appendix.

Reported speedups are substantial (up to ~13.7x rendering, ~2.5x training on MonoDyGauBench; up to 33x on individual HyperNeRF scenes) while largely maintaining PSNR/SSIM close to the DeformableGS baseline for the pruning-only configuration.

The temporal extension of Hessian/gradient-based sensitivity pruning (TSP) to the dynamic setting, and the self-supervised temporal jitter idea (TSS), are reasonable, low-overhead additions that plug into an existing pipeline without requiring extra supervision.

GroupFlow's grouping-via-trajectory-similarity and Umeyama-based rigid SE(3) fitting is a clean, interpretable way to compress N per-Gaussian deformations to J group transformations, and the paper shows it can have a mild regularizing effect in some noisy real scenes.
Clear writing and figures illustrating the qualitative effect of pruning/GroupFlow (floater suppression, Gaussian count reduction) support the quantitative claims to some degree.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental: TSP is a fairly direct temporal extension of existing static-scene Hessian/gradient pruning (PUP-3DGS, Speedy-Splat), and GroupFlow's clustering + shared rigid transform is conceptually close to prior group-based motion methods (SC-GS, RigGS, SPGaussian) cited by the authors; the paper does not clearly articulate what is technically novel beyond combining these ideas for the deformable-GS setting.

Quality claims are overstated in places: GroupFlow alone (without pruning) causes a non-trivial PSNR/LPIPS drop relative to baseline in several tables (e.g., 4DGS+GroupFlow on MonoDyGauBench drops PSNR from 23.55 to 21.00 and LPIPS from 0.277 to 0.380; iPhone dataset 4DGS+GroupFlow PSNR falls from 15.13 to 11.83), which sits awkwardly with the abstract's claim of 'preserving superior image quality' and 'surpassing all baselines in speed while preserving superior image quality.'

TSS's independent contribution appears marginal or inconsistent across tables (sometimes improving PSNR/SSIM slightly, sometimes slightly hurting LPIPS or FPS relative to TSP alone), undercutting the claim that it meaningfully stabilizes pruning; the paper does not provide a rigorous, isolated quantitative analysis of TSS's floater-suppression claim beyond one qualitative figure.

The comparison baselines for 'non-neural' efficiency are limited to the five methods already in MonoDyGauBench (EffGS, STG, STG-decoder, RTGS); no comparison is made to other recent efficient/compressed dynamic GS methods cited in related work (e.g., MEGA, temporally compressed 3DGS, LGS), despite being referenced, leaving the efficiency-fidelity frontier claim only partially substantiated.

No variance/statistical significance (e.g., standard deviation across the three repeated runs) is reported despite repeated-run averaging being emphasized, making it hard to judge whether reported gains (especially small PSNR/SSIM differences, e.g., TSS vs TSP-only) are meaningful or within noise.

Reproducibility is only partially supported: while hyperparameters (pruning percentages, β, τ, J) are specified, no code/checkpoint release is mentioned in the manuscript, and GPU heterogeneity across experiments (3090/A5000/A6000) for different metrics makes some reported multipliers harder to interpret cleanly as apples-to-apples comparisons.

The method is tied specifically to DeformableGS/4DGS-style explicit neural deformation fields; its applicability is explicitly limited to motion-field-based dynamic 3DGS variants (as stated in the Limitations), restricting generality claimed by the broad title 'Speedy Deformable 3D Gaussian Splatting.'

strengths: Extensive and thorough empirical evaluation across multiple datasets (NeRF-DS, D-NeRF, HyperNeRF, MonoDyGauBench's 50 scenes across 5 datasets), with per-scene breakdowns and multiple ablations (pruning percentages, number of groups) in the appendix, lending strong credibility to the reported speedups.

The three proposed modules (TSP, TSS, GroupFlow) are well-motivated extensions of existing static-scene techniques (Speedy-Splat/PUP 3D-GS pruning, SE(3) motion distillation) to the dynamic setting, with clear technical derivations (e.g., the second-order sensitivity score in Eq. 5-6) and sensible engineering choices (annealed timestamp perturbation, farthest-point-sampling-based grouping with Umeyama alignment).

Reported results are impressive and consistent: large rendering speedups (6.78x-13.71x on MonoDyGauBench, up to 33x on individual scenes) with minimal or even positive impact on image quality (SSIM/MS-SSIM sometimes improve over baseline), and substantial reduction in Gaussian count and model size, addressing a genuine and practically important efficiency bottleneck in neural deformation fields.
Good ablation coverage of design choices (group count J, soft/hard pruning ratios) that helps justify hyperparameter selections and demonstrates the sensitivity/robustness of the approach.

The paper is clearly written and well organized, with helpful figures (e.g., Fig 1-4) illustrating the pipeline and qualitative improvements, and the related work section appropriately situates the contribution relative to pruning and group-based motion literature.
weaknesses: The core technical contributions are largely direct adaptations of existing static-3DGS pruning techniques (Speedy-Splat/PUP 3D-GS Hessian-based sensitivity) and existing motion-clustering ideas (control-point-based skinning, SE(3) rigid grouping similar to SC-GS/RigGS) to the dynamic setting; the novelty is primarily in combination and temporal extension rather than a fundamentally new technique, which somewhat limits originality.

GroupFlow's performance trade-off is inconsistent and not fully explained: on DeformableGS/MonoDyGauBench it sometimes reduces PSNR/LPIPS quality noticeably (e.g., Table 2: PSNR drops from 23.86 to 23.52, LPIPS worsens from 0.295 to 0.313) while other times it improves SSIM/MS-SSIM; the paper attributes this to a 'regularizing effect' without rigorous analysis of when/why this occurs versus when it hurts (e.g., D-NeRF quality degradation in Table 8).

The method assumes locally rigid motion, which is explicitly flagged as a limitation for highly deformable/non-rigid regions, but the paper does not include any experiments explicitly probing scenes with challenging non-rigid deformation (e.g., cloth, fluid) to characterize failure modes beyond a brief textual acknowledgment.

Only DeformableGS and 4DGS are extended with the proposed pruning/GroupFlow modules; despite MonoDyGauBench identifying 5 representative motion parameterizations, EffGS, STG, and RTGS are not augmented, leaving open whether the approach generalizes to non-MLP/non-HexPlane motion representations.

Some experimental setup details raise minor reproducibility concerns: FPS/training time are measured across different GPUs (RTX 3090 for FPS, various A-series for training) and the MonoDyGauBench wrapper is noted to underperform the authors' own standalone codebase (Appendix A.6), which could complicate independent verification and fair comparison to the baseline numbers reported in the original benchmark paper.

The additional inference-time overhead from the pruning score/TSS computation and the flow-grouping distillation process (extra training stage, sampling of control points, Umeyama alignment) is not clearly quantified separately from end-to-end training time, making it harder to assess the added algorithmic complexity/overhead independent of the final speedup numbers.
